doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: September 11 and the call from Al Porcino
summary: Andre says it did not change his work, recalls Al Porcino's call from Munich and the Tom Harrell octet tape.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Wow. Fascinating. Sad. Let me wrap up here by asking if September 11th changed your life much, either from a music standpoint or in any other regards.

That’s a hard one. I mean I really don’t think so. Maybe I should see my analyst to be sure. I’m only kidding. I mean it was a terrible thing, an awful thing, as a matter of fact I’ll never forget the first phone call, well the first phone call that I got that morning, and I

had seen it on television, as a matter of fact it may have been happening, no it had just happened when I talked to this person, Al Porcino called me from Munich, Germany. Do you know the name Al Porcino?

He says, “Wayne, what’s—” And I don’t know Al Porcino that well. He says “Wayne, what’s going on over there? What in the world is this going on?” And we talked and talked and talked and talked. I says “Al, I don’t know, but I remember last night I subbed on Toshiko’s band and I remember seeing Jake Hanna at the bar and I remember seeing Jake Hanna dumping martinis down, and I’m wondering what in the hell he’s thinking about this morning. I never have spoken to Jake to find out, with this hangover he must have had with this going. One thing is being sober, but this thing is, but anyway Al Porcino called me because what happened is that as I say we don’t know one another that well. I mean we know each other professionally but he had recorded, I was over in Europe with Tom Harrell’s octet and he was in Munich the night we were there in this club and he had his tape recorder running. And I remember that night I felt good, I was on. Some nights I didn’t feel so good. But that night I felt really good about my playing. So actually I got his address from John Mosca and I wrote to him in 1997 to ask him if he would send me a copy of this tape. I never heard from him. Finally in 2001 he sends me this tape. He says “Oh I just came across this on my desk.” So I had received a tape and I can’t remember if I — I think I wrote him back to thank him for sending me the tape and had just heard from me so I was the closest one right after this happened, yeah. My son’s mother’s husband’s daughter’s husband, they haven’t found him yet. Now my son wasn’t really close to this guy but he knows pretty well his wife, but that’s the only close connection I have with anybody that was there. But as far as the music business goes I don’t think it’s changed the music business. It certainly hasn’t changed the music business for me. I mean it was a big thing with cutting salaries on Broadway for a while which I don’t really want to get into, but I think our union was a little intimidated by the stagehand union who always have a job. Musicians don’t always have a job. And when “Phantom of the Opera” and “Les Miserables” and I’m not there so I shouldn’t criticize what I don’t know, but when they’re making millions and millions of dollars and not passing the profits down to the musicians, all of a sudden they start to lose money, they want musicians to be their partner?
